claims.text: The equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets have distinct mechanical responses.
Constituent count alone is inadequate to explain the mechanical-property differences.
The compared quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
The alloys will be compared by uniaxial deformation under identical strain-rate and temperature conditions.
In situ high-energy diffraction and advanced microscopy will be used to monitor microstructural evolution.
The alloys differ in their local lattice distortions.
The alloys contain chemically induced short-range order that differs among compositions.
Local chemical environments produce composition-dependent heterogeneity in stacking-fault energetics.
Stacking-fault energy influences dislocation glide and deformation twinning.
The quinary alloy has a more heterogeneous local lattice-strain distribution than the ternary and quaternary alloys.
Greater chemical complexity in the quinary alloy promotes more short-range chemical ordering than in its subsets.
The quinary alloy's lattice-strain heterogeneity and short-range order lower the barrier for dislocation nucleation.
The quinary alloy's lattice-strain heterogeneity and short-range order lower the barrier for twin nucleation and facilitate twinning relative to the subsets.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have less heterogeneous lattice-strain fields.
Relative to the quinary baseline, the quaternary and ternary alloys will have higher barriers for twin formation.
The quaternary and ternary alloys will show strain-hardening rates and ductilities different from those of the quinary alloy.
The proposed mechanism applies at room or moderately elevated temperatures under uniform uniaxial deformation where dislocations and twins can be resolved.
The quantitative effects of lattice distortion and stacking-fault-energy variation on dislocation and twin nucleation thresholds remain uncertain.

The hypothesis would be falsified if the quinary alloy showed no statistically significant differences from the subsets in lattice distortion, stacking-fault energy, or dislocation and twin dynamics under identical tests.
